## 1. Macro regime check

FRED-derived indicators score this **supportive (4/5)**: Fed funds falling (3.62% vs 3.64% three months ago, as of 2026-07-10), HY credit spreads tightening (2.69% vs 2.84%), VIX falling (17.16 vs 18.36), NFCI loose (-0.52), yield curve not inverted (10y2y +0.35, though flattening from +0.50). SPY is above its 200-DMA (752.10 vs 692.03) and its 50-DMA (741.40), up 2.2% over the past month — a healthy uptrend, confirming benchmark_trend="supportive".

Two nuances worth flagging. First, the FRED CPI series still shows YoY *rising* (3.46% vs 3.29% three months ago, dated 2026-06-01), but today's live tape headline ("June CPI Falls More Than Expected") suggests the actual June print — released after that FRED series' last update — came in cooler than the market feared. I can't verify the exact number without a stale/lagged FRED read, so I'm not building any thesis on it, but it's a tailwind if true and consistent with today's broad tech strength. Second, 10Y yields are up to 4.56% from 4.31% three months ago — still a headwind for the richest multiples in the book (a reason to keep favoring reasonably-multipled names over 40-100x momentum names).

Net: regime supports normal aggression on quality AI-infrastructure setups, but the rising-yield backdrop argues for continuing to prefer names with real earnings support over story stocks.

## 2. Portfolio review

Two open positions, both opened this week, both healthy. No forced exits this run, no corporate actions.

**DELL — HOLD.** Bought 7/9 at $450.67 (4 days held), last $458.16-459.18, +1.7% unrealized. Stop cushion is 1.66x ATR (10.95% away, not inside the noise band). Chart shows a clean higher-low consolidation right at the rising 20-day average after the huge May-June run, with volume drying up on pullbacks (`no_supply_pullback` — constructive). Today's headline flow: "Insider Alert: Top Dell Insiders Cashes Out $27 Million" sounds alarming but checking `insider_activity.by_ticker.DELL`, 766 of the 772 sells in the last 120 days are Silver Lake (the founding PE sponsor) converting Class B to Class C and trimming — confirmed via web search: these are Silver Lake fund entities, not operating executives, selling down a legacy stake gradually since early July at prices $405-$450. Only 5 discretionary officer/director sells appear in the window. This is sponsor de-risking, not a signal the operators think the stock is overvalued — I'm not treating it as bearish. Fundamentals (current through Q ended 2026-05-01, not stale): operating margin improving (8.34% vs 4.98% a year ago), net debt/EBITDA a conservative 1.66x, shares outstanding shrinking 6.55% YoY on buybacks. The one soft spot: gross margin compressing (17.75% vs 21.12% four quarters ago) — consistent with the AI-server mix/pricing pressure I flagged at entry; watching for this to stabilize. No earnings until 9/3. Thesis intact, room to the $525 target remains; holding.

**HPE — HOLD.** Bought 7/10 at $48.85 (3 days held), last $49.51-49.67, +1.7% unrealized. Stop cushion 1.87x ATR (9.91% away). Chart shows a base building in the $44-52 range since the post-earnings/Juniper-close spike, today making a marginal new local high — no breakdown, no red flags. Fresh news confirms the thesis is still developing in my favor: HPE + NVIDIA won a large-scale AI data center deal with Vultr (shares +3-3.7% on the news last week) and a new Qblox hybrid quantum-computing partnership — both incremental proof points for the "AI-infrastructure reinvention" thesis, not just the Juniper cost story. Operating margin has swung from -14.5% to +7.0% YoY as one-time integration charges roll off. One thing to watch that I didn't weight heavily enough at entry: net debt/EBITDA is 4.36x ("levered" by the system's own scale) — HPE is not a clean balance sheet, and I'm holding this position on the earnings-recovery and multiple-re-rating thesis, not a fortress-balance-sheet argument. Insider activity is 12 of 13 sells being 10b5-1 plan trades (routine) — no cluster selling. Analyst target $64.13 (+29% from here) with a "buy" consensus. Thesis intact; holding.

Cash test: DELL's remaining path to its $525 target from $458 is ~15% over the remaining ~35 days of the horizon — comfortably above the 4% cash bar. HPE's path to $56.50 from $49.67 is ~14% over ~37 days — same. Both pass. Portfolio beta is elevated (1.78) but `shared_left_tail: false` (DELL/HPE pairwise correlation 0.61, not extreme) and both hold fresh, positive catalysts.

## 3. Universe scan — watchlist triggers

Two of my own prior watchlist levels are flagged as hit today. Neither is a clean confirmed entry yet.

**AMD** — parsed trigger $555, last $555.30 (+0.05%). But my own stated conditions were "above-average volume and MACD crossing positive, ideally after the 7/16 TSMC print." None of those confirm yet: `volume_surge_5d_vs_3m` is 0.59 (below average), MACD histogram is still below zero (state=`below_zero`, though rising), and ADX is only 22.0 (below the 25 threshold for an established trend — this is still chop by the indicator's own read). The move today is real and news-driven — Commerce Department approved AMD's MI308 shipments to select Chinese firms (ZTE, Kingsoft Cloud), confirmed via web search; BofA raised its target to $620 on the news. That's a genuine incremental catalyst on top of the existing 125% 3-month momentum and a fwd-PE/growth ratio near 1.0x (cheapest in its own peer group). But AMD's beta to the book is 3.35 — very high — and I don't have confirmation the move holds into the close or through tomorrow's TSMC print, which is the read-through catalyst for the whole complex. I'm not chasing an unconfirmed breakout on a partial trading session. Holding for confirmation.

**ANET** — parsed trigger $185, last $182.07 (-1.58%, so still below the level, not above it). My stated condition also required EPS revisions "stabilizing or turning positive again" — the 30-day revision is still slightly negative (-0.06%, essentially flat but not the turn I asked for). No entry.

Neither MU, RBRK, OKTA, nor NET (the rest of the standing watchlist) show a new trigger or a material change since this morning's write-up; MU bounced 4.9% today on the broader chip-sector strength but is still MACD-below-zero and 21.7% off its high — no reclaim yet.

Today's EDGAR 8-K sweep surfaced only FANG, TDG, and WMB — none are in the AI/data-center universe core focus and none warrant a look this run.

- AMD: Commerce Dept case-by-case export licensing shift confirmed live via web search (AMD MI308 shipments to ZTE/Kingsoft Cloud approved 7/14/26; BofA target raised to $620). Real, dated, verifiable catalyst — but see entry-quality discussion above.
- DELL: Silver Lake insider selling confirmed via web search to be sponsor share sales/B-to-C conversions dated 7/6-7/9, not fresh executive selling — consistent with my no-action read.
- HPE: Vultr/NVIDIA AI data center win and Qblox partnership confirmed via web search — both post-Juniper-close catalysts reinforcing the thesis.

## 5. Thesis & proposal

No new trades this run. Both open positions are working, within their swing horizon, and re-underwritten today with fresh data — holding both. The two watchlist names whose price levels were technically touched today (AMD, ANET) both fail my own stated confirmation conditions on volume/momentum/revisions, so I'm not forcing size into an unconfirmed move purely because a price alert fired. That discipline is the point of writing "would_buy_at" conditions in the first place.

The watchlist_trigger_alerts check only tests the price level, not the other stated conditions (volume, MACD, revisions) in the same "would_buy_at" text — today both AMD and ANET fired the price alert while clearly failing the qualitative conditions I wrote alongside it. It would help to parse and surface those secondary conditions (volume_surge, MACD state, EPS revision direction) alongside the price-trigger flag so the alert reads "price hit, but 2 of 3 conditions unmet" instead of just a bare price match — that would make the mid-day check faster without changing the discipline.

What I got right: discipline held under pressure - six separate runs today all correctly said no-trade rather than forcing a mediocre setup into a rate-driven, breadth-thin tape, and both live entries were valuation-anchored (12-20x forward earnings) rather than chases into the 40-170x names topping the momentum scan. What went wrong was mostly data quality, not reasoning: the insider Form-4 feed got flagged as noisy five separate times this week because financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's Dell unwind, ALAB's post-lockup sales) bury genuine officer-conviction signals under hundreds of routine rows, a stale next_earnings field showed a past date for HPE, and the post_earnings_drift_candidate flag missed HPE's textbook drift setup because a one-time GAAP charge masked rising estimates - all bad data, not bad judgment, but they cost research time I'd rather spend on names. The one change for next week: get the insider feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions before it's handed to me, since that single fix has been the most repeated friction point of the week and is pure engineering, not agent judgment.

** The insider_activity feed is dominated by financial-sponsor unwinds (Silver Lake's programmatic Dell distribution ran to 79 separate line items) and routine 10b5-1 officer sales, which bury any genuinely informative *open-market* signal. A pre-computed classifier flag distinguishing "sponsor/PE distribution" and "scheduled 10b5-1" from "discretionary open-market officer buy/sell," plus a net cluster-buy score, would let me weight this data in seconds instead of scrolling hundreds of near-identical sell tickets to conclude "no signal."

** The insider_activity feed lumps financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's DELL unwind, ALAB's pre-arranged director sales) in with genuine operating-insider signals, forcing me to manually parse dozens of near-identical rows to conclude "not a real signal." A pre-computed classification — tagging each cluster as sponsor/10b5-1-scheduled vs. discretionary officer transaction, and netting to a single per-ticker signal — would make the "clustered officer buying vs. routine selling" judgment the rules ask for far faster and less error-prone.

** The `post_earnings_drift_candidate` flag was `false` for HPE even though it fits the textbook drift profile the bundle prioritizes (record quarter just reported, +40% EPS revisions, price still 24% below its high). The detector appears to have been distorted by HPE's GAAP net *loss* last quarter — a one-time Juniper acquisition charge — which masked the underlying estimate momentum. Adding a "GAAP charge / acquisition-adjusted" screen (or keying the drift flag off EPS-revision magnitude and days-since-earnings rather than reported net income sign) would have surfaced this run's best idea automatically instead of leaving me to reconstruct it by hand.

** The context bundle's per-candidate `next_earnings` field is unreliable — HPE's showed `2026-06-01` (already past) while the `days_to_earnings`/`days_since_earnings` fields correctly implied the next print is in September. These two sources disagreeing forced me to reason around it; the run would be cleaner if `next_earnings` were validated to always be a *future* date (or dropped in favor of the days-based fields), so the earnings-clock gate can't be tripped by a stale value.

** The `insider_activity` feed is dominated by non-signal noise — Silver Lake's sponsor-distribution selling in DELL and Alba/Dyckerhoff post-lockup selling in ALAB swamp the data with hundreds of routine rows, which buries any genuinely informative *officer* buying/selling. This run would have been sharper if the context bundle pre-classified Form 4s (e.g., tagging financial-sponsor/10%-owner distributions and post-IPO-lockup sales separately from discretionary open-market C-suite transactions) and surfaced a net "discretionary officer" buy/sell tally per ticker, so clustered insider *conviction* signals aren't drowned out by mechanical unwinds.

** The context bundle gives me valuation and price/momentum but no consensus estimates or forward revenue-growth figures, so I'm forced to lean on trailing fundamentals plus headline sentiment when judging whether a rich multiple (ANET at 41x, ALAB at 97x) is justified. Adding forward revenue-growth and EPS-revision (analyst estimate trend) fields per candidate would materially sharpen the "is this multiple deserved" call and reduce reliance on qualitative news vibes — the single biggest lever on proposal quality this run.

** The context bundle deep-researches only the top-5 by deterministic score, but two of those five (TXN, AMD) are effectively un-actionable this run because of earnings timing (7/22) or a same-day news gap — meaning I burned my richest data (filings, 13F, news) on names I won't trade, while candidates like HPE and CRDO that I'm actively weighing had only a price and momentum row. Adding a `next_earnings` field and a `days_to_earnings` flag directly into the `universe_scan.top_setups` rows (not just the news block), plus expanding SEC/news enrichment to the top 8 rather than top 5, would let me screen out earnings-binary setups before spending research budget and give me fundamentals on the names I actually end up considering.

** This run would have been materially better with two data additions to the context bundle: (1) a **forward valuation field per candidate** (P/E or EV/S vs. its own 1-yr history) — right now I'm inferring "extended" purely from price momentum, when the real question for the CPI/rate-driven multiple-compression thesis is whether valuations are stretched, and (2) **intraday/1-day price change** so I can distinguish a name resting after a run from one spiking on news *today* (AMD) without cross-referencing headline timestamps by hand. Adding a `pct_change_1d` to the price block and a `valuation` sub-object to each `top_setups` entry would sharpen entry-timing judgment on exactly the chase-vs-wait decisions that dominated this cycle.
